label: paragraph_title
text: COAL WAR.

label: paragraph_title
text: FINAL RAY OF HOPE IN THE COMMONS.

label: text
text: General Strike Formally Proclaimed at Midnight.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons an animated discussion took place on the coal crisis.

label: text
text: The Chancellor of the Exchequer significantly hinted that the Government was prepared to resume the negotiations if the challenge of a general strike was withdrawn.

label: text
text: Mr. J. H. Thomas asked if this meant that the employers notices would likewise be withdrawn, but he did not press for an immediate answer.

label: text
text: A meeting was arranged subsequently between the member of the Cabinet and the Trades Union Congress.

label: text
text: It was announced at 11.30 p.m. that the negotiations had failed. A general strike was proclaimed at midnight.

label: text
text:
Notwithstanding numerous conversations between the members of the Cubine and the Trade Unionists in the House of Commons it was announced at 11:30 p.m. that the negotiations had failed.
A general strike was proclaimed at midnight.

label: text
text: STATE OF EMERGENCY.

label: text
text:
The House of Commons opened with the customary questions. The tenseness of the atmosphere was apparent from the cheering, counter-cheering, and laughter as the various party leaders entered.
Colonel Ashley announced that the Ministry of Transport had arranged for a service of motor cars to convey M.P.'s to and from Parliament.

label: text
text: Mr. S. Baldwin, Prime Minister, at the end of questions, presented a message from His Majesty the King declaring a state of emergency. He moved that a humble address be presented to His Majesty thanking him for the message.

label: text
text:
The Labourites insisted on a
division and the motion for the
address was carried, the voting
being:—

label: paragraph_title
text: Majority 200

label: paragraph_title
text: Mr. Baldwin's Statement.

label: text
text: Com. the Rt. Hon. B. M. Eyres-Monsell (Conservative, Evesham), moved the adjournment of the House, whereupon Mr. Baldwin, who received an ovation from the Ministerinlists, made a statement. He declared that the occasion was one of the gravest on which the House had ever met. He reviewed the difficulties of the coal industry, which were largely due to its own extraordinary machinery for the adjustment of wages. That machinery required radical overhauling, which would be one of the first things that must be tackled when the atmosphere was calmer. The owners and miners must find, or have found for them, some way of managing their own business independently of a Government intervention just like other great industries.

label: text
text:
The Risk He Ran
Mr. Baldwin dwelt on the risk he ran in negotiating up to the last minute under the threat of a general strike. (Ministerial cheers).

label: text
text:
The situation had changed materially on Sunday. Certain overt acts in anticipation of a general strike and involving interference with the freedom of the Press, occurred between 2 and 3:30 o'clock on Sunday (Labourite laughter).
That made the continuance of the negotiations impossible. The Government found itself challenged with an alternative Government.
Despite Power.
He (Mr. Baldwin) did not believe that there had been a thorough-going consultation with the rank and file before this despotic power was put into the hands of a small Executive in London. (Ministerial cheers)
This was a gross travesty of every democratic principle. The Labour leaders did not seem to realise that they were threatening the basis of ordered Government

label: text
text: and going nearer to proclaiming civil war than we had been for centuries.

label: text
text: The only light hearts in the country to-day were those which either envied or hated us because they saw our whole democratic freedom entering on a course which, if successful, could be the only substitute for tyranny.

label: text
text: It was not wages but the very freedom of our Constitution that was impelled. Everything for which he had worked and cared for during the past two years had been smashed to bits, but that did not shake his faith or the courage of his aims. (Ministerial cheers).

label: paragraph_title
text: LABOUR VIEW.

label: paragraph_title
text: "Not a Revolution" Shays, M.P. Thomas.

label: text
text: Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labourite, Derby) said that whatever might be the result of the strike anybody was a blind idiot who did not see that the economic facts of the coal position would remain. He did not believe that two per cent. of the population would support a revolution but people involved in the strike might be driven to circumstances that might have all the effects of a revolution with entirely different objects.

label: text
text:
"This is not a revolution, but a plain economic industrial dispute."
Parliament could force an honourable settlement, and he would make a contribution to that where ever the opportunity offered.

label: paragraph_title
text: AN APPEAL

label: text
text: Mr. D. Lloyd George (Liberal), Carnarvon), begged the Government be make one more effort for peace. He said that the members of the Trade Unions Congress who ordered the strike were as little revolutionary as anyone there, and the Government could continue the negotiations without any loss of its rights or position.

label: text
text: He proposed that the miners be asked to open the negotiations and discuss wages, but not to pledge themselves to a reduction in advance.

label: text
text: Will Government Make One More Effort?

label: text
text: He added that in the event of the resumption of the negotiations the House would agree to a limited continuation of the subsidy.

label: paragraph_title
text: NO HOT HEADS.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHANGE

label: text
text: See Reconstruction Programme

label: text
text:
Mr. J. Ramsay MacDonald (Labourite, Aberavon) solemnly asked the members of the House in their hour of trial to raise themselves to a great triumph. He declared that they were faced with a situation the development and end of which none could visualise.
If the miners were going to accept a reduction of wages on the programme of reconstruction they must see the programme of reconstruction first.

label: text
text: He respected the Constitution as much as the Conservatives, and whatever their differences they ought not to enter on the dispute with hot hands, but with a determination to do justice.

label: paragraph_title
text: PARTNERS?

label: paragraph_title
text: CHANCELLOR'S VIEW

label: text
text:
Miners Have Not Budget An Inch.
Mr Winston Churchill Chancellor of the Exchequer said gladly recognised that the Tra

label: text
text: Although "confirmation is lacking, there is no reason to doubt a report, from Canton, that Mr. Wong Ching-wai (erstwhile chairman of the Political Council) has left for Shanghai on a Russian vessel, the declared object of his trip being to go to Mostow to recuperate (after his recent reported illness).

label: text
text:
Mr. Wong's departure, if correct, synchronises with the return from Moscow of Mr. Hu Han-min. Before the first big coup of last summer, Mr. Hu had been governor of Kwangtung. When the system of government by commission was set up, Mr. Wong became chief civil politician by reason of his post. It is no secret that Mr. Hu then fell into disfavour with General Chang Kai-shek, who had just reached the head of affairs as the soldier of the hour.
About a month or so ago, Mr. Wong was reported to have sought privacy on account of his ill health. Since then he has taken little part, in public at least, in the administration. One of his last acts, it believed, led to the letter to Hongkong, asking for the appointment of three official delegates to meet three Canton officials in strike negotiations.

label: text
text: Rumours have been current that Mr. Wong has not seen eye to eye with General Chang (who is best known as commandant of the Whampoa Cadets).

label: text
text: A gentleman who is well touch with the position would not go so far as to say that General Chang had made overtures to Mr. Hu Han-min to cooperate with him. In his opinion that would be a natural inference as there is no denying that General Chang has the biggest say, directly or indirectly. He did not express any definite view regarding this latest report of political movements. There might be, he said, other reasons for Mr. Wong's departure than disagreement with General Chang and he thought that Mr. Wong's going to Moscow was unlikely to have been influenced by the General's attitude.

label: text
text: It is interesting to note that although an ardent revolutionary and republican long before the fall of the Manchu dynasty in 1911, Mr. Wong Ching-wai has hardly, if ever, been in office, until the death of Dr. Sun Yat-sen, when his leadership (as "President" or "Generalissimo") was succeeded by the form of government by commission.

text: A hydrant breakage near the sea wall, not far from the Hongkong Club, led to an escape of water which presented a geyser-like effect to those crossing the harbour this morning. It was some considerable time before the trouble was located, the water shut off and repairs effected.

text: Union negotiations had striven to ward off a shocking disaster to national life. The Government had also striven for peace by words and deeds.

text: He pointed out that all appears for more time meant a continuation of the subsidy. The Government would only agree to that if there were a real chance of settlement. He said that the miners had practically "not budgeted an incr since July. He did not believe that a continuation of the subsidy for a fortnight would clear up the position.

text: Withdraw the Challenged Mr. Churchill asked what Government could enter into partnership with a rival Government to sit in judgment on every train that ran?

label: text

The Government must shoulder the responsibilities even if it were necessary later to take steps which, if mentioned now, might seem drastic.
He added that the Trade Unions Congress had only to withdraw the challenge of a general strike and the Government would immediately resume with the most patiently labourious task of the past few weeks.

label: text
text: RAN INTO A WALL

label: text
text: Marine Lake was driving the cycle and Marine Jones occupied the billion seat. On taking a curve in the road, the machine suddenly swerved into a granite wall. The riders were both unsentenced and received severe injuries to the head, hands and neck by striking against the wall.

label: text
text: The cyclists were lying on the road in a helpless condition for some considerable time when a Chinese driving a motor cycle and side-car happened to come along. He promptly attended to the removal of the injured men to the Naval Hospital.

label: text
text: A Chinese emigrant was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with the unlawful possession of three revolvers and 929 rounds of ammunition.

label: text
text: Tendering a plen of guilty on behalf of the accused. Mr. J. T. Prior asked for a lenient sentence. He said the man was a butcher in America and returned by the s.s. "President Taft" on his way to the country: While in America, he had heard of the number of armed robberies committed in China and brought the weapons for his own protection. So far as he (Mr. Prior) was aware, the accused had not been in Hongkong for 30 years and he had been away from China for 15 years.

label: text
text: Sergeant McDonald said that inquiries made from reliable persons have been satisfactory to the police and he did not wish to press the charge.

label: text
text: His Worship imposed a fine of $500 and ordered the confiscation of the arms.

text: The nuisance caused by push cyclists in crowded thoroughfares was mentioned when a coolie stood charged with pushing another coolie off the machine at Queen's Road West, thereby causing bodily injuries.

text: Alleged to be property stolen from a show case at Queen's Road East, a young couple were charged with receiving a part of the jewellery. Mr. M. W. Lo, defending, pleaded not guilty.

text: Joss sticks wrapped in bundles and rolled in a blanket brought bad luck to the owner, a cook on the s.s. "Kinshan." Being too heavy for what they looked, the searchers cut the bundles open and found 14 taels of illicit opium hidden in the middle.

text: Instead of waiting for the American Consul to find him a passage somewhere, James Ronan, a seaman, was stated to have taken to drink, served a time in prison and then finished up in hospital.

label: paragraph_title
text: “A FIGMENT.”

label: text
text: COUNSEL ON TAM LAY'S "IMAGINATION."

label: text
text: "WONDERFUL STORIES."

label: text
text: The case for the defence of the second prisoner in the Wing. On Bank case opened this morning Mr. C. G. Alabaster describing the evidence "of Tam Lay, a crown witness as a "figment of the imagination" and as "wonderful stories" the evidence of Chung Sam, another Crown witness who stated that the second prisoner had confessed to him complicity in the alleged fraud.

label: text
text: Although the two prisoners appeared jointly, said counsel, it was the duty of His Lordship and the jury to enquire, severally into the evidence against them. The defence of the second prisoner was totally different from that of the first.

label: text
text: The first charge against him was that in conjunction with two other men he conspired to defraud the Wing. On Bank of $50,000 by means of forged books; that he did it in Hongkong (that was essential to the charge) and that he did it on divers dates not specified between March 1, 1923, and February 1, 1926. The prisoner's case was that he did not. It was not part of prisoner's case to say whether one or both books were either genuine or forged, continued counsel. He says he did not conspire in the making of those books either between those dates or at all.

label: text
text: The second charge against prisoner was that he (again in this Colony) in conjunction with another man, uttered, i.e., presented for payment, the book "Emma" on May 3 and thereby got what was known as the first withdrawal. His case was that he did not have anything to do with it. It was again no part of his case as to whether or not the books were forged.

label: text
text: The 3rd charge concerned the alleged withdrawals a day later. Prisoner denied that he had anything to do with the two later withdrawals.

label: text
text: The fourth count was that on August 14, 1923, he endeavoured in conjunction with the first prisoner to demand by means of the Industrial and Commercial Bank, the sum of $50,000 from the Wing On by virtue of the other book which the Crown alleged was forged in part ("Nina.").

label: text
text: It was not a part of prisoner's case whether the label of "Nina" was genuine or forged. He had nothing to do with it.

label: text
text: “Uncorroborated Evidence.”

label: text
text: The charges dated as far back as March 1, 1923 and some of the evidence dated back to October or November, 1922 and practically all the evidence brought with relation to the second prisoner consisted of the uncorroborated evidence of a man named Tam Lay who had stated that he joined the service of the second prisoner in October November, 1922 and remained there in connection with printing work in a shop in Canton until June 8, 1923.

label: text
text:
During that period certain things which Tam Lay and Tam Lay alone deposed to were said to have occurred. The defence to that was very simple. Tam Lay was not employed at the second prisoner's shop in Canton and never had been, as he had stated, said counsel.
Such a statement did not depend alone on the evidence of the second prisoner who was to be put into the box, but would be corroborated. Tam Lay had stated that the first prisoner and another man had a printing business in Tai Shan Street, Canton, called the Chung Wah, and that it was a printing business from the time he joined it in 1922 and throughout the period in question.
